traditions/old-order-mennonites/summary: Conservative Mennonites who resisted innovations such as Sunday schools, English-language preaching, revival meetings and new technology. The movement began with Jacob Wisler in Indiana and Ohio (1872), followed by Abraham Martin in Ontario (1889) and Jonas Martin in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (1893). Most groups still drive horse and buggy, though some (such as the Weaverland Conference) allow plain black cars.
traditions/old-order-mennonites/distinct: Separation from the world in dress, technology and language
Meetinghouses without Sunday schools or musical instruments
traditions/old-order-mennonites/profile/: Scripture, read through the Dordrecht Confession (1632) and the community's Ordnung (rules of practice).
Salvation by God's grace, received by faith and shown in obedience, humility and separation from the world.
Ordinances: adult baptism by pouring, the Lord's Supper twice a year, foot washing and the holy kiss.
Christ's return, resurrection and judgement, without detailed millennial schemes.
Bishops, ministers and deacons chosen by lot from among the men of the congregation; conferences keep a common Ordnung.
Slow unaccompanied hymn singing, long sermons and silent prayer in plain meetinghouses.
The 66-book Protestant canon, usually the Luther Bible or King James Version.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/summary: A Mennonite renewal church founded on 6 January 1860 in the Molotschna colony in the Russian Empire (now Ukraine), when eighteen men signed a document of secession calling for a converted membership. Influenced by German Pietism through the preacher Eduard Wüst, and by Baptists, they adopted baptism by immersion. Emigrants took the church to North America from the 1870s, and missions spread it to India, the Congo and beyond.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/distinctiv: Personal conversion as the condition of membership
Evangelical and Pietist warmth within Anabaptist teaching
Strong missionary work since the late nineteenth century
Global fellowship through ICOMB (International Community of Mennonite Brethren)
traditions/mennonite-brethren/profile/au: Scripture as the final authority, expressed in the Mennonite Brethren Confession of Faith.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/profile/sa: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, shown in a converted life and discipleship.
Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial; foot washing in some places.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/profile/es: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; views on the millennium vary.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/profile/go: Congregational, with national and provincial conferences.
traditions/mennonite-brethren/profile/wo: Evangelical services with singing, preaching and testimony; strong choral tradition among Russian Mennonite descendants.
traditions/wisconsin-lutheran-synod/summ: A confessional Lutheran church founded in Milwaukee in 1850 by German immigrant pastors led by John Muehlhaeuser. Initially moderate, it became strictly confessional under Adolf Hoenecke and joined the Synodical Conference with the Missouri Synod in 1872. It broke fellowship with Missouri in 1961 over doctrinal differences, especially on church fellowship, and leads the Confessional Evangelical Lutheran Conference founded in 1993.
traditions/wisconsin-lutheran-synod/dist: Strict doctrine of fellowship: no shared worship or prayer without full doctrinal agreement
Full subscription to the Book of Concord
Men only in the pastoral office and in roles of authority over men
traditions/wisconsin-lutheran-synod/prof: Scripture as the inerrant Word of God, with unconditional subscription to the Lutheran Confessions in the Book of Concord (1580).
Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, proclaimed through Law and Gospel.
Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper with the true body and blood of Christ really present, as means of grace.
Amillennial; Christ's visible return, resurrection and final judgement.
Synodical structure with a president, districts and a biennial convention; congregations call their pastors.
Lutheran liturgy and hymnody from Christian Worship (2021).
traditions/orthodox-presbyterian-church/: A small conservative Presbyterian church founded on 11 June 1936 in Philadelphia by J. Gresham Machen and others who had been removed from the northern Presbyterian Church for opposing theological liberalism. It is closely linked with Westminster Theological Seminary (1929), where Cornelius Van Til and John Murray taught, and is known for strict adherence to the Westminster Standards.
Strict subscription to the Westminster Confession and Catechisms
Strong emphasis on foreign missions, e.g. in Eritrea, Uganda and Japan
Scripture as the inerrant Word of God, with the Westminster Confession and Larger and Shorter Catechisms as subordinate standards.
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone, within Reformed covenant theology and predestination.
Baptism of believers and their children, and the Lord's Supper in which Christ is spiritually present to faith.
Mostly amillennial; Christ's return, resurrection and last judgement.
Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and a general assembly.
Reformed worship following the regulative principle, with psalms and hymns and expository preaching.
The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is excluded.
traditions/free-church-of-scotland/summa: Formed at the Disruption of 18 May 1843, when about a third of the ministers of the Church of Scotland, led by Thomas Chalmers, left over the state's interference in calling ministers (patronage). Most of the Free Church joined the United Presbyterians in 1900, but a minority, strongest in the Highlands and Islands, continued as the Free Church of Scotland. A further split in 2000 created the Free Church of Scotland (Continuing).
traditions/free-church-of-scotland/disti: Spiritual independence of the church from the state
Westminster Confession as the subordinate standard
Exclusive psalmody until 2010, when hymns and instruments were permitted
traditions/free-church-of-scotland/profi: Scripture as the supreme rule, with the Westminster Confession of Faith as the subordinate standard.
Salvation by grace alone through faith in Christ, in Reformed covenant theology.
Baptism, including infants of believers, and the Lord's Supper with Christ spiritually present, traditionally after preparatory services.
Christ's return, resurrection and final judgement; amillennial and postmillennial views both held.
Presbyterian: kirk sessions, presbyteries and a General Assembly.
Reformed worship centred on preaching; psalms (often unaccompanied) and, since 2010, hymns at congregational discretion.
traditions/reformed-presbyterian-covenan: Heirs of the Scottish Covenanters who refused the Revolution Settlement of 1690 because it did not uphold the National Covenant (1638) and the Solemn League and Covenant (1643). Followers of the martyrs Richard Cameron (killed 1680) and James Renwick (executed 1688) met in 'societies' until John McMillan and Thomas Nairn formed the Reformed Presbytery in 1743. Reformed Presbyterian churches now exist in Scotland, Ireland, North America and Australia.
Covenanting: public covenants binding church and nation to Christ
Christ's mediatorial kingship over the nations as well as the church
Exclusive singing of psalms without instruments
Historic political dissent from constitutions that do not acknowledge Christ
Scripture, with the Westminster Confession and Catechisms and each church's own Testimony as subordinate standards.
Salvation by grace alone through faith, in Reformed covenant theology.
Baptism of believers and their children, and the Lord's Supper with Christ spiritually present.
Christ's return and judgement; postmillennial hope for the nations has been prominent.
Unaccompanied singing of the psalms only, Scripture reading, prayer and preaching.
traditions/international-churches-of-chr: A movement that grew from the 'discipling' method of Chuck Lucas's Crossroads Church of Christ in Gainesville, Florida, and was launched by Kip McKean at the Lexington (later Boston) Church of Christ in 1979. It spread fast through planted churches in world cities and became separate from the mainline Churches of Christ. After McKean's departure (2001–2002) and an open letter by Henry Kriete (2003) criticising authoritarian practices, it was reorganised in 2006 as a cooperation of autonomous churches.
Baptism by immersion for forgiveness of sins after a commitment to be a disciple
Rapid planting of churches in major cities
HOPE worldwide, a charity founded in 1991
Reorganised in 2006 after criticism of its earlier hierarchy
The Bible alone as the guide, in the Restorationist tradition.
Faith, repentance, confession and baptism by immersion for the forgiveness of sins, followed by a life of discipleship.
Baptism of disciples by immersion and the weekly Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; little speculation on the millennium.
Autonomous congregations led by evangelists and elders, cooperating regionally and globally.
Sunday services with singing, communion and preaching, plus midweek groups.
traditions/congregacao-crista-no-brasil/: Brazil's oldest Pentecostal church, founded in 1910 by Louis (Luigi) Francescon, an Italian immigrant from Chicago who had been part of William Durham's Pentecostal mission. Beginning among Italian immigrants in São Paulo and Paraná, it grew into one of Brazil's largest Protestant churches while keeping a strikingly austere style: no paid clergy, no broadcasting and no organised evangelistic campaigns.
Unpaid ministry of elders (anciãos) and deacons
No radio, television or public evangelistic campaigns
Men and women sit apart and women wear veils
Large church orchestras and the hymnal Hinos de Louvor e Súplicas a Deus
A Calvinist-leaning stress on God's election, from Francescon's Presbyterian past
The Bible, with the brief 'twelve articles of faith' and guidance believed to come from the Holy Spirit.
Salvation by God's grace through faith in Christ, with a strong emphasis on God's election and calling.
Baptism of believers by immersion and the Santa Ceia (Holy Supper), celebrated once a year in each congregation.
Christ's return to gather the church, the resurrection and final judgement.
Elders and other ministers serve without pay; a council of elders in São Paulo (Brás) guides the church.
Hymns by number with orchestra, spontaneous prayer and preaching by those moved by the Spirit, without prepared sermons.
traditions/church-of-pentecost-ghana/sum: Ghana's largest Protestant church, founded by the Irish missionary James McKeown, who arrived in the Gold Coast in 1937 for the Apostolic Church of Bradford. After disputes with the parent church in 1953 he and most Ghanaian members formed the Gold Coast Apostolic Church, renamed the Church of Pentecost in 1962. Under Ghanaian leaders since McKeown's retirement in 1982 it has spread through West Africa and the African diaspora.
traditions/church-of-pentecost-ghana/dis: Leadership by apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, elders and deacons
Strong unpaid lay leadership by elders and deacons
Self-supporting from the start, with little foreign funding
Pentecost International Worship Centres (PIWC) for English-speaking and international congregations
Missions in more than a hundred countries
traditions/church-of-pentecost-ghana/pro: The Bible as the inspired Word of God, with the Apostolic Church's Tenets of faith.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with emphasis on holy living.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Premillennial; the Rapture of the church and Christ's return.
A centralised church led by a Chairman, General Secretary and Executive Council, with apostles over regions and pastors posted by the church.
Lively Pentecostal worship in Twi and other languages, with prayer for healing and deliverance.
